title: The Simca P60 Rush engine: what really changes after the Flash
author: Caramagnols
excerpt: The Rush keeps the Flash 1,290 cc engine’s principal dimensions but gains a five-main-bearing crankshaft and centrifugal oil cleaner. Identification, mechanical effects and buying checks.
content:
The change from Flash to Rush did not turn the P60 into a wholly new car. The four-cylinder retained a conventional layout, 1,290 cc capacity in its 7 CV forms, and 74 × 75 mm bore and stroke. The decisive alteration lies lower down: the Flash crankshaft runs in three main bearings, whereas the Rush has five. Simca also fitted a centrifugal oil cleaner at the end of the crankshaft.

These changes arrived in October 1960 for the 1961 model year. Factory material then used the Aronde Rush name, although P60 remained the everyday term for the body shape. For a buyer or restorer, the date affects the parts order, service schedule and value of an engine that genuinely matches the advertised version.

Why five main bearings matter

Each combustion stroke pushes through a piston and connecting rod to the crankshaft. Between supports, the shaft bends and oscillates slightly under combustion forces and the inertia of the moving parts. Two extra main bearings shorten the unsupported sections and place virtually one connecting rod between each bearing pair. A period technical road test reproduced by Club Simca describes this reduction in crankshaft oscillation as the central benefit of the Rush.

Better support chiefly brings reassurance at sustained speed and a stronger basis for long life. It should not be converted into a modern promise of silence or freedom from vibration. The camshaft remains in the block, driven by a chain, and operates overhead valves through tappets, pushrods and rockers. The Rush is an improved engine from the 1950s, complete with period mechanical noises and a need for regular adjustment.

The centrifugal cleaner changes servicing

The second distinguishing feature is the oil cleaner at the end of the crankshaft. Rotation throws contamination against the device’s inner wall, where deposits accumulate. This principle does not remove the need for suitable oil and timely changes. Nor will old sludge disappear simply because fresh lubricant has been poured into the sump.

On an unknown engine, very dark oil or missing service history calls for a controlled investigation. Cleaning the centrifugal unit should follow the manual for the exact engine and be entrusted to someone familiar with its removal, reassembly and tightening specifications. Improvised work at the crankshaft end can create leakage, incorrect assembly or a lubrication failure far more serious than the original deposit.

Rush, Rush Super and Rush Super M

Rush is not a single power output. The standard engine was fitted to cars including the 1961 Élysée. Sporting and upper-range models used more powerful developments; in September 1961 the Montlhéry Spéciale saloon and Monaco Spécial coupé appeared with the 70 bhp Rush Super M. The economy Étoile 6 occupied a different position, using a smaller 1,090 cc engine within the wider family.

A power figure in a classified advert therefore needs a version, carburettor, cylinder head and block reference behind it. Period SAE horsepower should not be compared directly with later DIN ratings. When deciding whether to buy, measured condition is more useful than a brochure number.

Identifying a Rush without trusting paint

The red rocker cover is the most frequently quoted visual clue. It is also extremely easy to repaint. The centrifugal cleaner, accessory arrangement and mechanical references are stronger evidence. A 1961 car may have received a replacement engine during its working life; that does not prevent enjoyable use, but the change belongs in the history file.

Before reaching a conclusion, photograph the complete engine bay, manufacturer’s plate and accessible markings. Do not publish a complete chassis number online. A Simca club or an engineer familiar with Arondes can compare the information with the model year, while a parts catalogue helps identify peripheral components.

Checks with the engine stopped

  • Oil: level, smell of petrol, water contamination, sludge beneath the cap and evidence of previous changes.
  • Cooling: hoses, radiator, water pump, signs of leakage and deposits within the circuit.
  • Ignition and carburettor: tidy installation, sound leads, free controls and no weeping fuel.
  • Mounting: engine supports, exhaust, cable routes and pipes free from rubbing.
  • History: machining invoices, bearing, piston and gasket references, and mileage since the work.

Starting an engine that has stood for years without checking lubrication and cooling can destroy in minutes the component being assessed. If its history is uncertain, establish that it turns freely, prime the oil system using an appropriate workshop procedure, and make the fuel supply safe before attempting the first start.

What a road test should reveal

From cold, note how quickly the oil warning light goes out, together with knocks and exhaust smoke. Once hot, watch the light or pressure at idle, coolant temperature, fresh leaks and noises that appear as the oil thins. A compression test performed under the same conditions on all four cylinders is usually more informative through the difference between cylinders than through one absolute figure.

The gearbox is a separate subject. The period test notes that the earlier transmission was retained and criticises the unsynchronised first gear and some gearbox noise. A crunch caused by poor technique should not be blamed on the engine; equally, a rumble that rises with engine speed does not necessarily originate in the transmission. An experienced ear can prevent an expensive diagnosis based only on impression.

Restore without destroying evidence

Before removing accessories, take dated photographs, label every connection and retain displaced parts. Measure before ordering: cylinder bores, crankshaft clearances, main-bearing condition, cylinder-head flatness and timing wear determine the actual programme. Fresh paint can conceal a tired unit, while a dirty but documented engine may be the sounder basis.

The Rush gave the P60 a better-supported bottom end and a characteristic centrifugal oil-cleaning system. Its historical importance comes from those engineering changes, not from the word “Rush” or a coat of red paint. The main Simca P60 page introduces the range, while the P60 body identification guide completes the mechanical inspection.
